newsitem.title: FRANCE: UK's Rifkind asks French support on Euro federalism.
newsitem.headline: UK's Rifkind asks French support on Euro federalism.

text.p: British Foreign Secretary Malcolm Rifkind appealed for support from France on Monday to prevent further erosion of the power of national governments and parliaments by creeping federalism in the European Union.

In a speech to the Institut Francais des Relations Internationales, Rifkind said Britain would not accept any EU decision on foreign affairs or immigration achieved by majority voting that fundamentally affected its national interest.
In a clear warning ahead of June's EU summit, which will map out the future shape of the EU, Rifkind indicated that the Maastricht treaty of 1991 fulfilled Britain's immediate needs.
"We see it as a durable and well-judged response to the ambitions, but also to the concerns, of our citizens which are deeply held and long lasting," Rifkind said.

"And when others seek to challenge the equilibrium of Maastricht, and to transfer still more power from the nation state to the European level through majority voting or communitisation, we are instinctively unimpressed."
The speech was the third in a series Rifkind is making in various European cities to spell out Britain's increasingly isolated and sceptical position in the EU.
He told his audience his concerns about excessive integration have found resonance in Sweden but "the response was less encouraging" in Germany.
France and Germany head the push towards a common EU currency, an issue which splits British Conservatives.

Rifkind said recently the government is "on balance hostile" to British membership but finance minister Kenneth Clarke has insisted that the option remains for Britain to join a single currency on January 1, 1999.
Rifkind said he believed history meant France would show greater affinity with Britain's viewpoint because of its strong attachment to a national parliament.
Britain's belief that the European Parliament was not ready to use its powers "responsibly" meant national parliaments must remain the true source of democratic legitimacy in the EU.
"We agree with France on the need to strengthen their collective voices too, by giving them a consultative role in areas like justice and home affairs...," Rifkind said.

Rifkind repeated Britain's strong opposition to an increase in majority voting -- whereby a member government can be overruled by a sufficiently large majority of other EU members -- especially in foreign policy areas.
"I do not believe Britain or perhaps France would ever be able to accept being overruled by a majority vote on a question where they had national interests at stake," he said.
He said Britons would not accept that changes to immigration rules covering Britain could be made by qualified majority voting in Brussels rather than by the British parliament.

But Rifkind said Britain remained committed to Europe's success, and accepted the right of the European Court of Justice to influence British affairs. The court has overturned a number of British legal decisions to the anger of government ministers.
"We cannot have a single market without an obligation to play by its rules; including accepting decisions we may not like from an independent court. There is no free ride to free trade," he said.
